header:
Date: 2026-06-03 14:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Joan Li (Redwood CSM), Priya Patel (Deepshield Security Lead), Daniel Kim (Deepshield Platform), Lena Ortiz (Deepshield CISO)
summary: Deep dive on on-prem / VPC security architecture for a private deployment. Covered network zoning, ingress patterns, egress controls, customer-managed KMS/HSM options, RBAC/SSO provisioning, audit log delivery, and compliance artifacts. Agreed next steps: share SOC2/ISO docs, deliver deployment diagram, schedule pilot, and exchange egress allowlist and SIEM endpoints.
topics: Ingress options (private endpoints vs reverse proxy)
Audit logs, retention, and SIEM integration
SOC 2 / ISO evidence and pen-test expectations
transcript:
[00:00:03] Alex Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Wednesday afternoon, really appreciate it. Quick roll call?
[00:00:12] Priya Patel: Hi, Priya here, security lead at Deepshield.
[00:00:15] Daniel Kim: Daniel, platform eng.
[00:00:18] Lena Ortiz: Lena, CISO.
[00:00:22] Samir Rao: Samir, solutions engineer Redwood. I'll be leading the architecture part.
[00:00:26] Alex Martinez: Agenda — we want to go deep on network zones, ingress/egress, KMS, and logging. We'll keep it pragmatic with an eye to SOC2/ISO requirements.
[00:00:40] Priya Patel: Sounds good. Our main asks: keys must be customer-owned (HSM), audit trail to our SIEM, and no outbound to the public internet except to allowlisted vendor endpoints.
[00:00:55] Samir Rao: Great — Redwood supports customer-managed keys in both Dedicated and Private. For Private we can integrate with AWS KMS CMKs or bring-your-own HSM via CloudHSM, we also support on-prem KMS proxies for airgapped setups.
[00:01:14] Daniel Kim: When you say KMS proxy — is that an agent, or do you rely on our existing endpoint? How is the traffic routed?
[00:01:24] Samir Rao: Good Q. For on-prem we run a small control-plane connector in your VPC which uses a mutually authenticated TLS tunnel back to the Redwood control plane if you opt-in. For full airgap, we offer an offline keywrap mode where the HSM signs key-wrap operations and we never see plaintext keys — think of it like a KMIP proxy. Sometimes the transcript says K-N-M-S which is odd, but the capability stands.
[00:01:48] Priya Patel: We need to confirm that plaintext model weights or inference cache are never written to external S3. All artifacts must remain inside our VPC/storage.
[00:01:58] Samir Rao: That's our typical config for Private: model artifacts are pulled into a customer storage bucket or NFS in your network. The runtime runs in your subnet. By default we don't push anything outside except optional metrics if you enable SaaS metrics.
[00:02:12] Lena Ortiz: On SOC2, we need the audit trail for admin activity and key usage for two years. Can Redwood provide detailed key usage logs with KMS request IDs?
[00:02:23] Alex Martinez: Yes — we can emit KMS event logs and admin activity to CloudWatch/Stackdriver or to your SIEM via our log forwarder. We also support file-based delivery if you prefer SFTP ingestion.
[00:02:36] Daniel Kim: How granular is RBAC? We want least-priv principle — infra ops can deploy models but only sec team can access audit exports.
[00:02:45] Samir Rao: RBAC is role-based at the API/token level; we support SSO via SAML and SCIM for provisioning groups. You can map groups to roles: deployer, operator, auditor. We also support attribute-based controls for model-level read/write separation.
[00:03:00] Priya Patel: SCIM sync is critical — we need automatic offboarding.
[00:03:05] Samir Rao: SCIM is supported — we can auto-provision into Red-Role groups. Small note: when we demo SCIM sometimes the username mapping gets funky, so we recommend a quick sync test.
[00:03:18] Alex Martinez: Okay, Samir will walk us through a reference network diagram.
[00:03:23] Samir Rao: Pulling up shared deck link: https://redwood.app/decks/deepshield-arch.pdf (shared). So picture three tiers: control-plane connector in a management subnet, runtime nodes in a private inference subnet, and a bastion/NAT for controlled egress. Ingress is either private endpoint (VPC Endpoint) or a reverse proxy in your DMZ that terminates TLS and forwards over private links.
[00:03:48] Daniel Kim: We prefer VPC endpoints to avoid public LB. Does Redwood require any inbound ports open from the internet?
[00:03:55] Samir Rao: No inbound from Internet for private deployment if you use VPC endpoints. For reverse-proxy option you will have an edge LB but you can terminate at your appliance. We do recommend a bastion for ops access, and we support session recording for SSH via our connector.
[00:04:10] Priya Patel: About egress — we plan to allowlist only a handful of vendor SaaS IPs and our SIEM ingest. Do you support FQDN-based allowlisting?
[00:04:19] Samir Rao: Yes, the egress proxy supports FQDN allowlist plus mutual TLS to vendor endpoints. We also support DNS filtering at the egress gateway for additional controls. One caveat: caching and KV cache calls from model runtime may hit external package repos if not locked down; we usually run private mirrors.
[00:04:39] Daniel Kim: Good to know. We will bring our internal proxy and mirrored repos in the pilot.
[00:04:44] Lena Ortiz: Pen testing — do you permit us to do a pen test on the private runtime? Any guardrails?
[00:04:50] Alex Martinez: Yes — we allow client-initiated VAPT with prior notice. We'll coordinate blast radius controls, and we have an operations contact for the window. We also have a standard pen-test agreement template.
[00:05:01] Priya Patel: How about firewalling — we run strict egress firewall rules at L4/7. Can Redwood runtime survive behind a stateful firewall that blocks unusual high TTL flows?
[00:05:12] Samir Rao: The runtime uses standard TLS 1.2/1.3 outbound to your KMS or control-plane. For large token streams, we support HTTP/2 and multiplexing — it keeps connections efficient. If your firewall terminates long lived flows, we can use keepalive and heartbeats to preserve sessions. Occasionally transcription shows 'keep up live' but it's meant to be keepalive.
[00:05:33] Daniel Kim: Audit log retention — we need immutable logs for two years with integrity checks. Can you sign logs or push to our WORM bucket?
[00:05:43] Samir Rao: We can export logs to your WORM storage or S3 with Object Lock. For additional integrity we support log signing (HMAC) before export. Logs include admin actions, model rollouts, key usage events, and per-token billing metadata (we can redact if needed).
[00:06:00] Priya Patel: Data residency — our EU customers' data must stay in EU region. Does Redwood let us pin regions for the control plane and runtime?
[00:06:09] Alex Martinez: Yes, Private deployments can be fully pinned. For hosted products we offer region selection but not full data residency guarantees. For Private we run everything in your chosen region or on-prem.
[00:06:20] Priya Patel: We have an external KMS operator — they require that KMS requests be originated from a static IP range. Can the control-plane connector NAT through a fixed egress IP?
[00:06:31] Samir Rao: Yes — you can route the connector through a NAT gateway with an Elastic IP or through a proxy with a static IP. We documented this pattern in the runbook.
[00:06:40] Lena Ortiz: How do you handle secrets and container images for runtime? We need image provenance and ephemeral secrets.
[00:06:47] Samir Rao: We recommend scanning images and pulling them from your private registry. Secrets are fetched from KMS at boot and stored in-memory only; we avoid writing secrets to disk. There is an option for in-memory-only key cache with TTL and policy controls.
[00:07:00] Daniel Kim: For model weights, what size footprints are typical? We're thinking of keeping GPU nodes in subnet with local NVMe.
[00:07:08] Samir Rao: We support local NVMe or mounted network storage. We prefer local NVMe for latency; if you use network storage ensure the subnet has sufficient bandwidth and that egress to storage endpoints is allowed.
[00:07:21] Alex Martinez: A quick detour to compliance evidence — we'll share the SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 cert. These cover our hosted control plane; we provide mapping documents for Private deployments to show control equivalency.
[00:07:34] Priya Patel: Please include map of controls where you say 'customer responsibility' vs 'Redwood responsibility'. That's important for our auditors.
[00:07:41] Joan Li: We'll attach the shared responsibility matrix to the folder.
[00:07:45] Priya Patel: On RBAC and approval workflows — can we have an approval step before a model rollout goes into prod?
[00:07:51] Samir Rao: Yes — rollouts can be gated by approvals. We integrate with ticketing systems to require an approval event before a canary expands. There is also a webhook for your CI/CD system.
[00:08:04] Daniel Kim: About network microsegmentation — any recommendations? We want to limit east-west.
[00:08:10] Samir Rao: Create security groups per role: control-plane, runtime, inference-proxy. Use host-based firewall plus VPC NACLs for an extra layer. We also recommend service mesh for internal comms if you need L7 mTLS inside.
[00:08:24] Priya Patel: SIEM ingestion — format? JSON logs or syslog?
[00:08:29] Samir Rao: We support JSON over HTTPS, syslog, and S3 batched delivery. For real-time ingestion use HTTPS with mutual TLS. Format docs: https://redwood.app/docs/logschema (shared).
[00:08:40] Lena Ortiz: If we rotate keys frequently, does that disrupt runtime sessions?
[00:08:46] Samir Rao: We use envelope encryption. Rotating CMKs does not rekey in-memory caches immediately; we have a key rotation policy that handles rewraps gracefully. There can be a short window but we support zero-downtime rewraps with staged rotation.
[00:08:59] Priya Patel: Are there audit hooks for model outputs for compliance review? We need to sample generated outputs in certain regulated flows.
[00:09:07] Alex Martinez: We can enable structured output logging and sampling. You can set retention and redaction rules to avoid PII capture.
[00:09:15] Daniel Kim: Anything about bandwidth or throttling when we run heavy inference?
[00:09:20] Samir Rao: Autoscaling policies apply on the runtime; network egress is throttled per policy. We can honor your QoS profiles. For large batch jobs we recommend a private burst pool to avoid hitting egress limits.
[00:09:35] Priya Patel: Ok let's scope the pilot: 3 GPU nodes in our EU-prod-like VPC, KMS via our CloudHSM, logs to our SIEM over mutual TLS, and pen-test window after stabilization.
[00:09:47] Alex Martinez: Sounds good. We'll produce the diagram and the security folder. Anything else?
[00:09:52] Priya Patel: One last Q — who has access to the raw debug logs? We need to restrict dev access to PII.
[00:09:58] Samir Rao: Debug logs are access-controlled. By default only your auditors and our ops on a break-glass basis can fetch them; we record those events. We can redact or mask PII at ingress if you want.
[00:10:10] Lena Ortiz: Thanks. We'll follow up with the allowlist and SIEM endpoint.
[00:10:14] Alex Martinez: Great, I'll follow up with the SOC/ISO artifacts and the runbook.
[00:10:18] Joan Li: I'll create the shared folder and invite everyone.
[00:10:22] Priya Patel: Thanks everyone.
[00:10:25] Meeting end: short wrap, agreed next steps recorded above. (Note: several parts of the transcript had minor auto-caption errors, e.g., 'K-N-M-s' instead of KMS, 'keep up live' for keepalive.)
